pos: n. pl. (the lower grades of the Western clergy — porter, lector, exorcist and acolyte — below the major orders of subdeacon, deacon and priest)
etymology: Latin ordines minores, the lesser orders; ordo, a rank or row, used from the third century of grades within the clergy.
biblical_def: By the fourth century the Western church had four grades below the major orders: the porter who kept the doors, the lector who read the lessons, the exorcist, and the acolyte who carried lights and served the altar. Each had a rite of admission in which the candidate was handed the instrument of his office — keys, a book, a book of exorcisms, a candlestick. By the later Middle Ages all four had become stages a man passed through on his way to the priesthood in a single afternoon, and the duties were done by others. The New Testament knows differing functions in a congregation and lists them without grading them into a ladder: “God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues” (1Co 12:28). The word helps sits in that list without apology. Romans makes the same point about gifts: “Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us” (Rom 12:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines order as a rank, class or grade of men, and in ecclesiastical use the degrees of the clergy; and acolyte as an inferior church servant who attends the priest.
webster_full: ORDER, n. A rank, class or division of men; as the order of nobles. In ecclesiastical affairs, a degree in the ministry; as holy orders.
ACOLYTE, n. In the ancient church, one of the subordinate officers who attended the priest, lighted the candles, and performed other inferior services.
LECTOR, n. A reader; one whose office in the ancient church was to read the Scriptures in public worship.
PORTER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.
ORDINATION, n. The act of conferring holy orders or sacerdotal power; the act of setting apart to an office in the Christian ministry.
scriptures: And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.
Rom 12:6
Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith;
Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
corruption_summary: Four lower clerical grades whose offices had become stages passed through in an afternoon.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the ladder. Once functions in the church are arranged as grades, each one becomes a step toward the next rather than a work to be done, and the man ordained exorcist in the morning and acolyte in the afternoon has not exorcised or served anything. The apostolic correction is the body figure, in which the humbler members are not lower rungs: “those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary” (1Co 12:22).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the stated purpose of the arrangement of gifts, which is the opposite of ranking: “That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another” (1Co 12:25). A church with a ladder has a built-in schism, because every man on it is looking upward.
roots_summary: Latin ordines minores, lesser orders; Greek antilepsis (G484), helps; Greek kubernesis (G2941), governments; Greek charisma (G5486), a gift of grace; Greek schisma (G4978), a division.
roots_lines: Latin ordo — a rank, a row; whence order and ordination.
Greek antilepsis (G484) — a laying hold of, helps; “helps, governments” (1Co 12:28).
Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; “gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us” (Rom 12:6).
Greek asthenes (G772) — weak, feeble; “which seem to be more feeble, are necessary” (1Co 12:22).
Greek schisma (G4978) — a rent, a division; “That there should be no schism in the body” (1Co 12:25).
usage: “And God hath set some in the church” (1Co 12:28) — the setting is God's, not a ladder's.
“are necessary” (1Co 12:22) — said of the feeble members.
“the same care one for another” (1Co 12:25) — what a graded clergy makes hard.

pos: n. (a clergyman of the grade below deacon, who prepared the vessels and read the epistle; counted a major order in the West from the thirteenth century)
etymology: Late Latin subdiaconus, from sub, under, and diaconus, a deacon, from Greek diakonos, a servant or minister.
biblical_def: The subdeacon prepared the chalice and paten, poured the water, read the epistle at mass and assisted the deacon. The office appears at Rome in the third century, and in 1207 Innocent III counted it among the major orders, so that a subdeacon was bound to celibacy and to the daily office. The New Testament has deacons but no sub-deacons, and what it says about the diaconate is almost entirely about character and testing: “Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:8), and then the procedural rule that no church may skip: “let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless” (1Ti 3:10). The promise attached is also worth noting against a system of grades, because it does not promise promotion: “they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus” (1Ti 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subdeacon as in the Romish church, an under deacon, one who serves next under the deacon; and deacon as a person in the lowest degree of holy orders, and in Scripture one who serves tables.
webster_full: SUBDEACON, n. In the Romish church, an under deacon; one who serves next under the deacon.
DEACON, n. A person in the lowest degree of holy orders. In the primitive church, deacons had the charge of the alms of the church and the care of the poor.
GRAVE, a. Of weighty character; worthy of respect; of dignity or importance; not light, trifling or jocose.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard.
DEGREE, n. A step; a rank or station in life. A measure of advancement; a grade.
scriptures: Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;
And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.
For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
corruption_summary: A grade below deacon invented by the church, and the apostolic rules about the office it sits under.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the office multiplied past the point where anyone can be tested for it. Paul's requirement is that a deacon be proved first, which assumes a congregation that knows the man; by the thirteenth century a subdeacon could be a youth ordained in a cathedral by a bishop who had never met him. The test did not disappear from the books; it disappeared from practice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that character qualifications precede office, and that the congregation does the looking: “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business” (Act 6:3). The apostles appointed; the church looked out. Neither step can be done at a distance, and the reward offered to a faithful deacon is “great boldness in the faith” (1Ti 3:13) rather than a higher rung.
roots_summary: Latin subdiaconus, under-deacon; Greek diakonos (G1249), a servant; Greek semnos (G4586), grave or venerable; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to prove; Greek parrhesia (G3954), boldness.
roots_lines: Latin subdiaconus — under the diaconus or deacon.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, a minister; the root of the whole office.
Greek semnos (G4586) — grave, honourable; “must the deacons be grave” (1Ti 3:8).
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; “let these also first be proved” (1Ti 3:10).
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; “and great boldness in the faith” (1Ti 3:13).
usage: “not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:8) — a character test, not a grade.
“being found blameless” (1Ti 3:10) — the condition of use.
“look ye out among you” (Act 6:3) — the congregation does the looking.

pos: n. (the third of the Western minor orders, admitted by the handing over of a book of exorcisms; an office that retained its title long after it had lost its function)
etymology: Greek exorkistes, one who administers an oath or adjures, from exorkizo, to bind by oath; the word appears once in the New Testament, and not favourably.
biblical_def: The minor order of exorcist was conferred by handing the candidate a book of exorcisms with the words that he should have power to lay hands on the possessed, whether baptised or catechumens. In practice, from an early date, actual exorcisms were performed by priests under the bishop's licence, and the minor order became a title held for an afternoon on the way to the priesthood. The New Testament uses the word exactly once, of men who had no business with it: “certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth” (Act 19:13). The result is one of the most alarming scenes in Acts. The spirit answers “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?” (Act 19:15), and then “the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded” (Act 19:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exorcist as one who pretends to cast out evil spirits by adjuration; and adjure as to charge, bind or command on oath, or under the penalty of a curse.
webster_full: EXORCIST, n. One who pretends to expel evil spirits by conjuration, prayer and ceremony.
EXORCISM, n. The expulsion of evil spirits from persons or places by certain adjurations and ceremonies.
ADJURE, v.t. To charge, bind or command on oath, or under the penalty of a curse.
POSSESSED, pp. Held; occupied; enjoyed. Affected by demons or invisible agents.
FORMULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model.
scriptures: Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.
And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
corruption_summary: A minor order whose book of exorcisms was handed to men who would never use it, and the one exorcist the New Testament names.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the formula used as a technique. The sons of Sceva had the right name and the right words and no relation to the person named, and the evil spirit says so in the sharpest sentence in the chapter: “but who are ye?” (Act 19:15). Authority over spirits is not transmitted by a book, a title or a correctly pronounced name, and a church that confers the office as a formality has taught precisely the opposite.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is our Lord's own correction of disciples who had genuinely cast out devils and were pleased about it: “Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luk 10:20). The authority was real and the warning was still necessary. Power over the enemy is never the believer's ground of confidence; his name in the book is.
roots_summary: Greek exorkistes (G1845), an exorcist; Greek horkizo (G3726), to adjure; Greek pneuma poneron, an evil spirit; Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to overpower; Greek ischuo (G2480), to prevail.
roots_lines: Greek exorkistes (G1845) — one who adjures; “certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists” (Act 19:13).
Greek horkizo (G3726) — to bind by an oath, to adjure; “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth” (Act 19:13).
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know by experience; “Jesus I know, and Paul I know” (Act 19:15).
Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to master, to overcome; “and overcame them” (Act 19:16).
Greek apographo (G583) — to enrol, to write down; “because your names are written in heaven” (Luk 10:20).
usage: “took upon them” (Act 19:13) — an office assumed, not given.
“naked and wounded” (Act 19:16) — the result of a borrowed formula.
“in this rejoice not” (Luk 10:20) — said to men whose power was real.

pos: n. (the porter or ostiarius, the first of the Western minor orders; he kept the church doors, rang the bells and opened the book for the preacher)
etymology: Latin ostiarius, from ostium, a door; the English porter is from porta, a gate, and renders the same office.
biblical_def: The ostiarius or porter was the lowest of the minor orders, and at his ordination the bishop handed him the keys of the church with the charge to open the house of God to the faithful and close it against the unworthy, to ring the bells, and to open the book for the preacher. The office is the only one of the four with a clear Old Testament ancestry, for the temple had porters in large numbers, ordained by David and Samuel: “All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office” (1Ch 9:22). The office also has the most famous line in the Psalter attached to it, said by a man kept outside: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10). The comparison is between the meanest place inside and the best place outside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doorkeeper as a porter, one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment; and threshold as the door-sill, the entrance or gate of a house.
webster_full: DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.
PORTER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.
THRESHOLD, n. The door-sill; the plank, stone or piece of timber which lies at the bottom or under a door, particularly of a dwelling house, church, temple or the like.
COURT, n. In Scripture, an enclosed space or yard belonging to the tabernacle or temple.
TABERNACLE, n. A tent. A temporary habitation. Among the Israelites, a movable building, so contrived as to be taken to pieces with ease and reconstructed.
scriptures: All these which were chosen to be porters in the gates were two hundred and twelve. These were reckoned by their genealogy in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office.
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Psa 84:2
My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God.
For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
corruption_summary: The porter with the church keys, the one minor order with a temple ancestry, and the psalm of a man outside the door.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the doorkeeper who forgets which side of the door he is guarding — the office of admitting and excluding, exercised for reasons the Scripture does not supply. A church door closed against the poor, the unfashionable or the inconvenient is being kept by a porter who has substituted his own list for his bishop's. The psalm's whole force depends on the house being open to someone who longs for it: “My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD” (Psa 84:2).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's arithmetic, which values the lowest position in God's house above the best elsewhere, and the promise that follows it: “no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly” (Psa 84:11). A man content to keep a door in that house has understood something about the house. The office is low and the location is everything.
roots_summary: Latin ostiarius, a doorkeeper; Hebrew shoer (H7778), a porter or gatekeeper; Hebrew saph (H5592), a threshold; Hebrew chatser (H2691), a court; Hebrew kasaph (H3700), to long for.
roots_lines: Latin ostiarius — from ostium, a door; the porter of the minor orders.
Hebrew shoer (H7778) — a gatekeeper, a porter; “chosen to be porters in the gates” (1Ch 9:22).
Hebrew saph (H5592) — a threshold, a doorway; the word behind doorkeeper in the psalm.
Hebrew chatser (H2691) — a court, an enclosure; “fainteth for the courts of the LORD” (Psa 84:2).
Hebrew tamim (H8549) — upright, complete; “them that walk uprightly” (Psa 84:11).
usage: “than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10) — the whole comparison.
“did ordain in their set office” (1Ch 9:22) — porters ordained by a king and a prophet.
“no good thing will he withhold” (Psa 84:11) — the promise to the man at the door.

pos: n. (the conflict between popes and emperors, roughly 1075 to 1122, over whether a lay ruler might invest a bishop or abbot with the ring and staff of his office)
etymology: From investiture, Latin investitura, a clothing or putting on, from investire, to clothe — the act of putting a man into his office.
biblical_def: The investiture controversy turned on a ceremony. When a bishop was appointed, someone handed him the ring and pastoral staff that signified his spiritual office; and since bishops held vast lands of the crown, kings had long done the handing. Gregory VII forbade it in 1075, Henry IV defied him, and the quarrel ran through excommunications, an emperor standing in the snow at Canossa, an antipope, and a civil war, to the compromise of Worms in 1122: the emperor gave up ring and staff and kept the right to invest with the temporal regalia. The underlying question is older than either party. Uzziah entered the sanctuary to burn incense and the priests withstood him: “It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed” (2Ch 26:18). And the Lord's own division of jurisdictions remains the rule: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines investiture as the act of giving possession of a manor, office or benefice; and regalia as ensigns of royalty, the rights and prerogatives of a king.
webster_full: INVESTITURE, n. The act of giving possession of a manor, office or benefice. The right of giving possession of a benefice.
REGALIA, n. Ensigns of royalty; the apparatus of a coronation; as the crown, scepter, etc.
CROSIER, n. A bishop's pastoral staff; a symbol of pastoral authority and care.
TEMPORAL, a. Pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular; as temporal concerns, temporal power.
SPIRITUAL, a. Consisting of spirit; not material. Pertaining to sacred things or to the church.
scriptures: And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.

Then Uzziah was wroth, and had a censer in his hand to burn incense: and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the LORD, from beside the incense altar.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: Half a century of war over who hands a bishop his ring, and the older question of two jurisdictions.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs both ways and this dictionary will not pretend it ran only one. A crown that appoints bishops will appoint useful ones; a papacy that forbids it, and then appoints bishops who hold armies and counties, has not resolved the problem but relocated it. Uzziah's trespass is the clearest case, and its outcome is a warning about office taken by rank: “the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the LORD, from beside the incense altar” (2Ch 26:19).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that both jurisdictions are ordained and neither may absorb the other. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) is written under a pagan emperor and gives the magistrate a real, divinely given authority. “and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21) fences it. The Reformed tradition has argued about where the fence runs ever since, and has never argued that it is not there.
roots_summary: Latin investire, to clothe; Hebrew qetoreth (H7004), incense; Hebrew maal (H4603), to trespass; Greek apodidomi (G591), to render; Greek exousia (G1849), authority.
roots_lines: Latin investitura — a clothing, a putting into office.
Hebrew qetoreth (H7004) — incense; “to burn incense unto the LORD” (2Ch 26:18).
Hebrew maal (H4603) — to act treacherously, to trespass; “for thou hast trespassed” (2Ch 26:18).
Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to render; “Render therefore unto Caesar” (Mat 22:21).
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, right; “For there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1).
usage: “go out of the sanctuary” (2Ch 26:18) — the priests to a king, and they were right.
“the things which are Caesar's” (Mat 22:21) — a real and limited claim.
“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — written under Nero.

pos: n. (a formal agreement between the papacy and a civil government regulating the affairs of the church within that state)
etymology: Medieval Latin concordatum, a thing agreed, from concordare, to agree, from cor, the heart — a meeting of hearts.
biblical_def: A concordat is a treaty between a church and a state. The Concordat of Worms in 1122 ended the investiture quarrel; the Concordat of Bologna in 1516 gave the king of France the nomination of his own bishops; the Lateran Treaty of 1929 made peace between the papacy and Mussolini's Italy; the Reichskonkordat of 1933 was signed with Hitler's government within six months of its coming to power, and the German bishops were left with a document and without a voice. The pattern is old enough to have an Old Testament case. Jehoshaphat was a good king who made an alliance with Ahab, and the prophet met him on the road home: “Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD” (2Ch 19:2). Amos asks the question that settles the matter of alliances in principle: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concordat as an agreement made by a prince with the pope relative to the collation of benefices; and treaty as an agreement, league or contract between two or more nations.
webster_full: CONCORDAT, n. An agreement made by a prince with the pope, relative to the collation of benefices; or a compact between the pope and a sovereign.
TREATY, n. An agreement, league or contract between two or more nations or sovereigns, formally signed by commissioners properly authorized.
ALLIANCE, n. The union between nations, contracted by compact, treaty or league.
ACCOMMODATION, n. Adjustment of differences; reconciliation; as of parties in dispute.
COMPACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a word that may be applied, in a general sense, to any covenant or contract.
scriptures: And Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to king Jehoshaphat, Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
corruption_summary: The treaty between a church and a state, and the prophet who met a good king coming home from one.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the security bought with silence. A concordat secures something real — schools, appointments, property, the right to exist — and the price is almost always a limit on what the church may say about the government that granted it. The case of Jehoshaphat is instructive because he was genuinely godly and the alliance was sealed by a marriage that looked like statesmanship: “Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab” (2Ch 18:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is not that the church must refuse all dealings with states, which is impossible, but that it must not place its confidence in them. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3) is the rule, and Amos supplies the test for any particular agreement: two cannot walk together unless they are agreed, so the honest question about a concordat is what has been agreed to.
roots_summary: Latin concordatum, a thing agreed; Hebrew azar (H5826), to help; Hebrew yaad (H3259), to appoint or agree; Hebrew nadib (H5081), a prince; Hebrew chathan (H2859), to join by marriage.
roots_lines: Latin concordare — to agree, from cor, the heart.
Hebrew azar (H5826) — to help, to support; “Shouldest thou help the ungodly” (2Ch 19:2).
Hebrew yaad (H3259) — to appoint, to meet by agreement; “except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3).
Hebrew chathan (H2859) — to make oneself a relative by marriage; “and joined affinity with Ahab” (2Ch 18:1).
Hebrew nadib (H5081) — a noble, a prince; “Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3).
usage: “therefore is wrath upon thee” (2Ch 19:2) — said to a good king about an alliance.
“Can two walk together” (Amo 3:3) — the question to ask of every concordat.
“in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3) — the limit of any treaty.

pos: n. (the formal curse of the church, pronounced with ceremony against heresy or contumacy, and distinguished in canon law from simple excommunication)
etymology: Greek anathema, a thing devoted to destruction; in the Septuagint it renders Hebrew cherem, the ban, and it is the New Testament word for accursed.
biblical_def: In canon law the anathema is excommunication with the solemnities: bells, book and candle, the candle cast down and extinguished, the formula pronounced by a bishop with twelve priests. It was aimed at heresy and at defiance of the church's judgement, and the conciliar canons of the Middle Ages and of Trent attach it to specific doctrinal propositions. The word itself is apostolic and Paul uses it twice with great weight. Of any man preaching a different gospel he says “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — and he includes himself and an angel in the hypothesis, which is the strongest way to say that the gospel outranks the messenger. Of the man without love to Christ he writes “If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha” (1Co 16:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines anathema as excommunication with curses, and a curse or denunciation by ecclesiastical authority; and imprecation as the act of imprecating or invoking evil on any one.
webster_full: ANATHEMA, n. Excommunication with curses. Hence, a curse or denunciation by ecclesiastical authority, accompanying excommunication.
IMPRECATION, n. The act of imprecating, or invoking evil on any one; a prayer that a curse or calamity may fall on any one.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
CONTUMACY, n. Stubbornness; unyielding obstinacy. A wilful contempt and disobedience to any lawful summons or judicial order.
MARANATHA, n. The Lord comes, or has come; a word used by the apostle Paul in expressing a curse.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Gal 1:9
As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.
If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.
Rom 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
corruption_summary: The solemn curse of the church, and the apostolic word it borrows, which Paul applies first to himself hypothetically.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the anathema deployed for jurisdiction rather than for the gospel. The medieval curse fell on men who refused a court's summons, withheld a payment or defied a legate, and it fell with the same words used against denying the resurrection. Paul's anathema is tied to one thing only, and he repeats it so it cannot be mistaken: “If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:9).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the temper in which such a word may be said at all, and Paul supplies that too. The man who wrote let him be accursed also wrote, of his own countrymen who had rejected Christ, “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom 9:3). Anyone who can pronounce an anathema cheerfully has disqualified himself from pronouncing one.
roots_summary: Greek anathema (G331), a thing devoted to destruction; Hebrew cherem (H2764), the ban; Greek euaggelion (G2098), the gospel; Aramaic maran atha, the Lord comes; Greek euchomai (G2172), to wish or pray.
roots_lines: Greek anathema (G331) — a thing devoted, hence accursed; “let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a thing under the ban, devoted to destruction.
Greek euaggelion (G2098) — good news, the gospel; “any other gospel unto you than that ye have received” (Gal 1:9).
Aramaic maran atha — our Lord comes; “let him be Anathema Maranatha” (1Co 16:22).
Greek euchomai (G2172) — to wish, to pray; “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ” (Rom 9:3).
usage: “though we, or an angel from heaven” (Gal 1:8) — the apostle includes himself.
“If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ” (1Co 16:22) — the one other ground.
“for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom 9:3) — the required temper.

pos: n. (the greater excommunication, which cut a man off not only from the sacraments but from the society and civil dealings of Christians; distinguished from the minor excommunication)
etymology: Latin excommunicatio major, from ex, out of, and communio, communion — the greater putting-out of communion.
biblical_def: Canon law distinguished two censures. The minor excommunication barred a man from the sacraments; the major cut him off from the fellowship of Christians altogether, so that others might not eat with him, trade with him or greet him, on pain of incurring the censure themselves. It was a fearsome instrument and it was used for debt and contempt of court as well as for sin. The New Testament has the procedure and gives it one purpose. Our Lord sets out the steps and the end: “if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17). Paul applies it at Corinth with a stated aim that is entirely remedial: “To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus” (1Co 5:5), and the congregation's duty is plain: “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1Co 5:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excommunication as the act of ejecting from a church, expulsion from the communion of a church and deprivation of its rights; and censure as a judicial sentence, judgment that condemns.
webster_full: EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church; expulsion from the communion of a church, and deprivation of its rights, privileges and advantages.
CENSURE, n. A judicial sentence; judgment that condemns. An ecclesiastical reprimand or penalty.
INTERDICT, n. In the Romish church, a prohibition of the pope, by which the clergy are forbidden to celebrate divine service, or to administer the sacraments.
RESTORE, v.t. To bring back to a former good state; to repair; to recover.
DISCIPLINE, n. Correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors.
scriptures: And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.
But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
corruption_summary: The greater censure, cutting a man off from Christian society, and the apostolic discipline that exists to restore him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is discipline used as a weapon of the court rather than a medicine for the soul. A censure pronounced for an unpaid fee, or against a whole town under an interdict so that infants went unbaptised and the dead unburied, has nothing in common with the apostolic practice but the vocabulary. The purpose at Corinth is stated in the same sentence as the sentence: “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus” (1Co 5:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the restoration that is the normal expected outcome. Paul writes to the same church about the same man and commands them to receive him back: “ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2Co 2:7). A church that can excommunicate and cannot restore has only half the ordinance, and the half it has will harden into cruelty.
roots_summary: Latin excommunicatio, a putting out of communion; Greek ekklesia (G1577), the church; Greek paradidomi (G3860), to deliver up; Greek exairo (G1808), to put away; Greek charizomai (G5483), to forgive freely.
roots_lines: Latin ex + communio — out of communion.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — the assembly, the church; “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17).
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to hand over, to deliver; “To deliver such an one unto Satan” (1Co 5:5).
Greek exairo (G1808) — to remove, to put away; “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1Co 5:13).
Greek charizomai (G5483) — to forgive, to show favour; “ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him” (2Co 2:7).
usage: “as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17) — the last step, after three others.
“that the spirit may be saved” (1Co 5:5) — the purpose, in the sentence itself.
“swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2Co 2:7) — the danger of discipline without restoration.

pos: n. (a sin whose absolution is withheld from the ordinary confessor and reserved to a bishop, a penitentiary or the pope)
etymology: From Latin casus reservati, reserved cases — sins whose remission the ordinary priest may not grant without a superior's faculty.
biblical_def: Reserved cases are sins which an ordinary priest may not absolve. The lists varied by diocese and era and included such things as striking a cleric, heresy, procuring abortion, forgery of papal documents and violation of the seal of confession; the penitent had to be referred upward, sometimes to Rome, where a department of the curia existed to handle them. The system was defended as a deterrent and as a safeguard of serious discipline. The doctrinal objection is not about the list. It is that forgiveness has been made an administrative good with grades of access. The scribes asked the right question of Christ, though for the wrong reason: “who can forgive sins but God only?” (Mar 2:7). Their premise was correct and their conclusion wrong, because the man before them was God. And the promise given to the penitent has no reservations in it: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1Jo 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines absolution as acquittal, the remission of sins, or of the punishment due to sins, pronounced by a priest; and penitentiary as an officer in the Romish church appointed to judge in matters of conscience.
webster_full: ABSOLUTION, n. In the civil law, an acquittal or sentence of a judge declaring an accused person innocent. In the Romish church, a remission of sins pronounced by a priest in favor of a penitent.
PENITENTIARY, n. In the Romish church, an officer appointed to judge in matters of conscience, and grant absolutions in reserved cases.
RESERVE, v.t. To keep in store for future or other use; to withhold from present use for another purpose.
CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment; the acknowledgment of a crime or fault. In the Romish church, a disclosure of sins to a priest.
CLEANSE, v.t. To purify; to make clean; to remove filth or foul matter of any kind.
scriptures: Mar 2:7
Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Isa 55:7
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
Psa 32:5
I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
corruption_summary: Sins the parish priest could not absolve, referred upward to a bishop or to Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is forgiveness administered in grades. Once some sins require a higher official, pardon has become a commodity with a distribution system, and the sinner's access to God depends on the rank of the man he can reach. The system was also, inevitably, a revenue stream: the penitentiary at Rome issued dispensations for a fee. Isaiah knows no such arrangement, and his invitation is addressed to the worst case: “let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” (Isa 55:7).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the directness and the completeness of the promise. David's account of his own pardon has no intermediary and no delay in it: “I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin” (Psa 32:5). The confession is to the LORD and the forgiveness arrives in the same sentence. John adds that God is not merely willing but “faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1Jo 1:9) — faithful to a promise, and just because the price was paid.
roots_summary: Latin casus reservati, reserved cases; Greek aphiemi (G863), to send away, to forgive; Greek homologeo (G3670), to confess; Hebrew salach (H5545), to pardon; Hebrew nasa (H5375), to lift away.
roots_lines: Latin casus reservati — cases reserved to a superior's absolution.
Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, to remit; “who can forgive sins but God only?” (Mar 2:7).
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to say the same thing, to confess; “If we confess our sins” (1Jo 1:9).
Hebrew salach (H5545) — to forgive, to pardon; “for he will abundantly pardon” (Isa 55:7).
Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift, to bear away; “and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin” (Psa 32:5).
usage: “and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1Jo 1:9) — all, with nothing reserved.
“he will abundantly pardon” (Isa 55:7) — abundance is the opposite of rationing.
“I said, I will confess” (Psa 32:5) — and forgiveness in the same verse.

pos: n. (the English statutes, chiefly of 1353 and 1393, penalising the pursuit of suits in a foreign court or the introduction of papal authority prejudicial to the crown; also the offence and its penalty)
etymology: From the opening words of the writ, praemunire facias, cause him to be forewarned; a scribal form of praemonere, to forewarn.
biblical_def: Praemunire took its name from a word in the writ and became the English crown's standing weapon against papal jurisdiction. The penalty was severe: forfeiture of all lands and goods and imprisonment at the king's pleasure. In 1529 Henry VIII charged Wolsey with praemunire for exercising his legatine authority, and in 1531 he charged the entire English clergy with it, extracting a vast fine and the first acknowledgment of his headship of the church. The statutes framed a question the church has had to answer since Jerusalem: what happens when two authorities both claim to bind. Peter and the apostles gave the answer under arrest: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Paul gave the other half to a church under Nero: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1). Both are in the canon and neither cancels the other, which is why the hard work is in distinguishing which case is before you.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines praemunire as the offense of introducing foreign authority into England, and the writ and penalty thereon; and allegiance as the tie which binds the citizen or subject to the government.
webster_full: PRAEMUNIRE, n. In English law, the offense of introducing foreign authority into England, the papal power being particularly intended. The writ grounded on the statute, or the penalty incurred.
ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; the duty of fidelity to a king, government or state.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.
FORFEITURE, n. The act of forfeiting; the losing of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office or effects, by an offense, crime or breach of condition.
SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:7
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
corruption_summary: The English writ against foreign jurisdiction, used by Henry VIII to charge his whole clergy at once.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the use of a genuine principle as a lever. The English objection to appeals abroad had real substance; a kingdom may fairly decline to have its land law decided in another country. But the statute as Henry used it in 1531 was an instrument of extortion against men who had done nothing new, and the supremacy it purchased was a transfer of exactly the kind of power the statute complained of, from a pope to a king.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing. Paul commands the payment of what is owed to the magistrate in detail — “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour” (Rom 13:7) — and the three in Babylon show the limit, refusing the image with no assurance of rescue: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18). Obedience is the rule; the exception is confessed openly and the penalty accepted.
roots_summary: Latin praemunire facias, cause him to be forewarned; Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; Greek hupotasso (G5293), to be subject; Greek opheile (G3782), a due; Aramaic pelach, to serve or worship.
roots_lines: Latin praemunire facias — the opening words of the writ.
Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to place under, to be subject; “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).
Greek opheile (G3782) — a debt, a due; “Render therefore to all their dues” (Rom 13:7).
Aramaic tselem — an image; “nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18).
usage: “rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the exception, stated under arrest.
“honour to whom honour” (Rom 13:7) — the rule, stated in detail.
“But if not” (Dan 3:18) — obedience without a guarantee of rescue.
